identification.summary: Red Menshen is a China-nexus threat actor tracked by PwC, which published on the group in 2022 and assesses it is almost certainly China-based [S2][S7]. It is best known for BPFDoor, a passive Linux backdoor that uses a Berkeley Packet Filter to inspect traffic at kernel level and wait for a trigger packet [S1][S3]. Its main targets are telecommunications providers [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly reported in 2022 (PwC TROOPERS 2022 talk; CFR dates its entry May 2022). A 2021 first-seen date could not be confirmed [S2][S7].
identification.notes: Trend Micro tracks the same activity as Earth Bluecrow [S1]. Malpedia lists Red Dev 18 and DecisiveArchitect as synonyms; CrowdStrike's 2022 report on DecisiveArchitect and its JustForFun implant is listed there [S7]. Malpedia is an aggregator, so treat vendor cluster equivalence as unconfirmed until the vendor reports are compared [S7]. The imported record has no Microsoft actor name and no MITRE group ID; none was found in sources reviewed.

attribution.confidence: PwC assesses the group is almost certainly China-based [S2][S7]. Rapid7 describes it as a China-nexus actor [S3]. One analysis noted no direct evidence linking the group to a specific Chinese military or intelligence entity, and a CFR entry lists China as the suspected state sponsor [S7]. No government attribution was found in the sources reviewed.
attribution.basis: Vendor assessments only (PwC, Trend Micro, Rapid7) [S1][S2][S3]. PwC also noted weekday-only activity, mostly 01:00-10:00 UTC, consistent with an 8 to 9 hour working window [S2][S7].

objectives: Long-term espionage access to telecommunications networks, with the aim of spying on corporate and government entities, as described by Rapid7 [S3].

regions: South Korea, Hong Kong, Myanmar, Malaysia, Egypt (2024 activity per Trend Micro) [S1]
South Korea and Taiwan network-edge appliances (Rapid7, 2026) [S5][S6]
targeting.notes: Telecoms are the core target, with government, education and logistics also named [S2][S7]. Trend Micro telemetry showed telecom, finance and retail victims in 2024, e.g. telecom in South Korea (July and December 2024), Hong Kong (January 2024) and Myanmar (December 2024), a Malaysian retail case in October 2024, and an Egyptian financial case in September 2024 [S1]. PwC's slides also list the USA; this was only seen in a search summary [S7].

capabilities.summary: Signature tool is BPFDoor, a passive kernel-level Linux implant that opens no listening port and waits for a crafted trigger packet [S1][S3]. PwC reported post-exploitation with custom Mangzamel (including Golang variants), custom Gh0st, Mimikatz and Metasploit against Windows systems [S7]. Trend Micro found a controller able to open a reverse shell for lateral movement [S1]. Rapid7 (March 2026) reported about 300 samples, seven new variants (F to L), and two primary variants, httpShell and icmpShell, that hide the trigger in HTTPS traffic or relay over ICMP [S3]. Reporting says initial access often comes via internet-facing edge devices (Ivanti, Fortinet, Palo Alto, routers, VMware ESXi were cited in one summary, with no specific CVEs confirmed), followed by CrossC2, Sliver and TinyShell [S3]. Rapid7 (October 2026) found a new BPFDoor variant and BPF-enabled Rekoobe posing as the Korean anti-spam product SpamSniper, and an SMTP-speaking implant, AVERAT, on Taiwanese appliances [S5][S6]. C2 reportedly ran through VPS servers administered via compromised Taiwan-based routers used as VPN tunnels [S2][S7].

diamond.adversary: China-nexus actor assessed by vendors; no named government sponsor or individuals in reviewed sources [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: BPFDoor passive implant and variants, controller, Mangzamel, Gh0st, Mimikatz, Metasploit, CrossC2, Sliver, TinyShell, Rekoobe, AVERAT [S1][S3][S5][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: VPS servers administered through compromised Taiwan-based routers acting as VPN tunnels [S2][S7]; compromised edge appliances and mail gateways as footholds [S3][S5].
diamond.victim: Telecommunications providers primarily, plus government, education, logistics, finance and retail, across Asia, the Middle East and Egypt [S1][S2][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage against corporate and government entities via telecom networks [S3].
diamond.technology: Linux servers and network-edge appliances with trust in existing open ports, SSL offload, and mail-gateway traffic that mask implant traffic [S3][S5].

gaps: WebFetch could not reach any vendor host (DNS failure), so all content comes from search-result summaries; primary Rapid7, Trend Micro, PwC and CrowdStrike documents were not opened.
No government attribution or sponsoring agency found; no Microsoft actor name or MITRE group ID found.
Specific CVEs for initial access are unconfirmed; vendor product names came from a secondary summary.
Alias equivalence (Earth Bluecrow, Red Dev 18, DecisiveArchitect) rests on Trend Micro and Malpedia; cluster boundaries not independently compared.
Exact publication dates for PwC and CrowdStrike 2022 reports, the Rapid7 March 2026 report day, and The Hacker News day were not confirmed.
Whether US targets were affected is unverified (PwC slide listing seen only in a summary); the Taiwan router relays may be victims or Red Menshen assets.
A Rapid7 whitepaper URL was removed because the URL was not seen in search results (the observed whitepaper URL differs); its claims remain supported by S3. PwC 2021 first-seen claim unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Telecom core and edge Linux servers, mail gateways, VPN/firewall appliances and routers are key cyber terrain; they carry traffic and subscriber data for host-nation and coalition partners in Asia and the Middle East [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2: The implant evades perimeter controls by hiding in existing ports and mail or HTTPS traffic, so defenders get little network visibility [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 3: Observed template is edge-device foothold, then CrossC2/Sliver/TinyShell, then BPFDoor persistence, with weekday 01:00-10:00 UTC operator hours [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet telecom espionage and tooling refresh in Asia. MDCOA is use of the same persistent access to monitor or disrupt partner-nation communications during a regional crisis (inference, not sourced). Candidate indicators: unexpected raw-socket/BPF filters on Linux hosts, daemon names mimicking SpamSniper, outbound SMTP-like sessions from appliances on TCP 25, ICMP relay between hosts [S1][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation telecom and edge-appliance compromises reported by vendors and feed them to the common operating picture [S1][S5]. (2) Authorities: hunting on partner or commercial telecom infrastructure needs host-nation or owner consent; clarify before any action. (3) Mission assurance: assume Linux edge appliances supporting mission communications may be implanted; verify with kernel/BPF-level inspection rather than port scans [S1][S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs and sector contacts; vendor detections (YARA/Suricata) came from Rapid7 for customers [S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Since 2021, Red Menshen, a China based threat actor, which has been observed targeting telecommunications providers across the Middle East and Asia, as well as entities in the government, education, and logistics sectors using a custom backdoor referred as BPFDoor. This threat actor uses a variety of tools in its post-exploitation phase. This includes custom variants of the shared tool Mangzamel (including Golang variants), custom variants of Gh0st, and open source tools like Mimikatz and Metasploit to aid in its lateral movement across Windows systems. Also, They have been seen sending commands to BPFDoor victims via Virtual Privat Servers (VPSs) hosted at a well-known provider, and that these VPSs, in turn, are administered via compromised routers based in Taiwan, which the threat actor uses as VPN tunnels. Most Red Menshen activity that has been observed took place between Monday to Friday (with none observed on the weekends), with most communication taking place between 01:00 and 10:00 UTC.131 This pattern suggests a consistent 8 to 9-hour activity window for the threat actor, with realistic probability of it aligning to local working hours.
